title: Guru Hargobind Ji: Miri-Piri, Akal Takht and the Response to 1606
intro: LESSON 20 | 7–10 minute reading | After Guru Arjan's death in Lahore in 1606, his young son Guru Hargobind inherited leadership of a Sikh community that had experienced direct Mughal punishment. His response is remembered through Miri-Piri, the Akal Takht, and the development of armed self-defence. These changes were not a rejection of Gurbani or of the earlier Gurus; they added visible temporal responsibilities to an already established spiritual and communal tradition. Central question: What changed after 1606, and which elements of the familiar stories can historians independently establish?
record:
DATED TIMELINE
1595 — Guru Hargobind is born, traditionally at Guru ki Wadali near Amritsar.
1604 — The Adi Granth is installed at Harmandir Sahib under Guru Arjan.
1606 — Guru Arjan dies in Mughal custody at Lahore. Guru Hargobind becomes the sixth Guru, traditionally aged about eleven.
c. 1606–1609 — The Guru's wearing of two swords and the development of the Akal Takht are traditionally dated to this period; exact dates and ceremonial dialogue are not independently documented.
1609 — Common traditional date for establishment of the Akal Takht, facing Harmandir Sahib in Amritsar.
1606–1627 — Jahangir's reign overlaps with the early Guruship; the Guru's confinement at Gwalior is usually placed within this reign, but exact years vary widely across sources.
1627 — Jahangir dies; Shah Jahan succeeds in 1628.
1630s — Armed confrontations under Shah Jahan belong to a later phase and will be studied separately.

THE SUCCESSION IN 1606
Guru Hargobind was the son of Guru Arjan and Mata Ganga. The fifth Guru's death was a watershed because Jahangir's own memoir acknowledges punitive imperial action against Guru Arjan, although historians disagree over the precise relationship between religious hostility and the Khusrau rebellion. Hargobind's succession took place amid this new danger. Sikh historical literature associates his accession with a conscious decision to maintain armed retainers and defend the community. Avoid assuming that every later ceremonial detail is attested by a contemporary eyewitness. The historical development is clearer than the exact words reportedly spoken at the accession.

MIRI AND PIRI: TWO KINDS OF RESPONSIBILITY
The two swords associated with Guru Hargobind signify Miri (temporal or worldly authority) and Piri (spiritual authority). In the Sikh tradition they express a refusal to separate religious commitment from responsibility for justice and protection. The swords should not be interpreted as an instruction to attack people of other religions. Sikh history includes relations of cooperation as well as conflict with Muslim rulers and religious figures. Nor was the concern with worldly life wholly new: Guru Nanak had criticised political oppression, and the succeeding Gurus had founded towns, maintained langar and organised congregations. The change under Hargobind was the more explicit assertion of temporal authority and the organised capacity for defence.

THE AKAL TAKHT AND HARMANDIR SAHIB
The Akal Takht, literally the 'Throne of the Timeless One', is associated with Guru Hargobind and commonly dated to 1609. It stands across from Harmandir Sahib in the Amritsar complex. In Sikh historical understanding the two spaces articulate complementary dimensions: the singing and hearing of Gurbani, and the public deliberation of communal matters. Early traditions associate the Guru with sitting on a raised platform, receiving visitors, hearing petitions and encouraging martial training. The present building has undergone later destruction and reconstruction, so its current appearance must not be mistaken for a photograph of the 1609 structure. The title and institutional standing of the Akal Takht also developed across subsequent Sikh history; avoid projecting every modern procedure back into Guru Hargobind's day.

A COMMUNITY CAPABLE OF DEFENCE
Accounts describe Guru Hargobind maintaining horses, weapons and armed followers, encouraging horsemanship and martial practice. These were material commitments: animals required feed, riders required training, and retainers needed support. A community that had already developed networks of offerings, towns and local congregations had some capacity to sustain them. The new armed organisation was not yet the Khalsa created under Guru Gobind Singh in 1699. It is equally inaccurate to treat the sixth Guru's following as a modern standing national army. Its scale and exact numbers are difficult to verify, especially when later biographies supply dramatic totals.

THE POLITICAL SETTING
Jahangir ruled the Mughal Empire until 1627. Guru Hargobind's leadership unfolded in the shadow of his father's death but cannot be reduced to uninterrupted war against Jahangir. Traditions preserve periods of tension and also accommodation. The later clashes commonly associated with the sixth Guru occurred principally under Shah Jahan, who became emperor in 1628. Keeping those reigns separate prevents anachronism. The broader historical question is how a growing religious community negotiated autonomy within a powerful empire.

GWALIOR: A REAL PLACE, A COMPLEX CHRONOLOGY
Sikh tradition remembers Guru Hargobind's imprisonment at Gwalior Fort and his eventual release. Scholars generally accept a period of confinement, but the precise date, duration, political cause and the number of fellow prisoners freed are not uniformly established. Some popular accounts give exact years or a fixed number of months without identifying a contemporary source. We should not silently choose one. The story's most familiar version concerns the Guru's refusal to leave without other captive rulers; this is considered below as a sakhi rather than a verbatim administrative record.

WHY THE CHANGE MATTERED
The first five Gurus had created a recognisable body of Gurbani, a succession of Gurus, an important centre at Amritsar, and a network of congregations. After 1606, the Guru's leadership visibly included the protection and public standing of the Panth. The Akal Takht became a durable symbol of collective authority. This development helped shape later Sikh responses to imperial pressure, but it is essential to study the later seventeenth century on its own terms rather than treating 1606 as if it already contained every feature of eighteenth-century Sikh power.

KEY PEOPLE AND PLACES
Guru Hargobind (1595–1644), sixth Guru; Guru Arjan, fifth Guru and father; Mata Ganga, mother; Baba Buddha, senior early Sikh; Bhai Gurdas, early Sikh writer; Jahangir, Mughal emperor until 1627; Shah Jahan, emperor from 1628; Amritsar, centre of Harmandir Sahib and Akal Takht; Gwalior Fort, site of the imprisonment tradition; Guru ki Wadali, traditional birthplace.

SOURCE NOTES
The original Gurbani of Guru Nanak, Guru Arjan and other Gurus remains the spiritual foundation of the community. The Miri-Piri swords and Gwalior episode are historical traditions, not verses to which an Ang number can honestly be assigned. No fabricated scriptural quotation is offered here. J. S. Grewal's The Sikhs of the Punjab treats the transition in the chapter on the Sikh Panth in the seventeenth century; Khushwant Singh, A History of the Sikhs, volume I, covers the sixth Guru and Mughal relations. Read both critically alongside the Encyclopaedia of Sikhism entries on Guru Hargobind and Akal Takht. Basics of Sikhi's WhyGuru material provides a Sikh devotional framing; it is valuable but not a substitute for evaluating the date and provenance of individual narratives.
tradition:
SOURCE-BASED SAKHI — BANDI CHHOR, THE RELEASE OF CAPTIVES
Later Sikh tradition describes Guru Hargobind imprisoned in Gwalior Fort. When permission to leave was granted, the Guru reportedly insisted that other imprisoned rulers should also be released. A well-known retelling says that a specially made robe with multiple tassels allowed the captives to hold on as they departed. This narrative is commemorated in Bandi Chhor Divas ('Day of the Liberator') and is especially associated with Gwalior and Amritsar. It teaches a remembered example of concern for others, but historians must separate the general tradition of detention and release from the precise number of prisoners (often given as 52), the robe design, the exact dialogue and the date. These particulars are not securely attested by a surviving contemporary court transcript. Consult the Encyclopaedia of Sikhism's entries on Guru Hargobind and Bandi Chhor Divas, and compare later Sikh narratives rather than presenting one version as an eyewitness record.

DISTINGUISHING EVIDENCE
Strong historical framework: Guru Hargobind succeeded Guru Arjan in 1606; his period was marked by a more overt temporal and defensive dimension; the Akal Takht is closely associated with his Guruship. Traditional detail: exact sword-girding conversations, Gwalior release dialogue, precise prisoner count and the robe. Uncertain chronology: dates and length of Gwalior detention. Next lesson will study Gwalior and Bandi Chhor in greater depth, followed by the conflicts of the 1630s under Shah Jahan.

The Akal Takht, traditionally established around 1609 opposite Harmandir Sahib, became associated with the public authority of the Panth. Horsemanship, weapons and armed followers signal an organised capacity for defence, not the later Khalsa of 1699. The Gwalior imprisonment and Bandi Chhor narrative are important Sikh traditions, but exact dates, prisoner numbers and speeches are disputed or not independently documented. Jahangir ruled until 1627; the major battles associated with the sixth Guru belong to the reign of Shah Jahan. NEXT — Lesson 21: Gwalior Fort, Bandi Chhor Divas and the limits of the historical record.

title: Guru Hargobind Ji: Gwalior Fort, Bandi Chhor Divas and the Mughal Court
period: c. 1606–1627 CE (Jahangir's reign; detention chronology disputed)
intro:
LESSON 21 — EVENING, 4 NOVEMBER 2026 | 7–10 MINUTE READ

Last time we examined Guru Hargobind Ji's accession in 1606, the two swords of Miri and Piri, the Akal Takht and the emergence of a more visible capacity for self-defence. Today we examine a famous episode whose precise chronology is much harder to reconstruct: the sixth Guru's confinement at Gwalior Fort and his remembered role in freeing other captives. The guiding question is: what can historians establish about Gwalior, and what does Bandi Chhor Divas commemorate?

Imagine the contrast between Amritsar, where Guru Hargobind led a growing Sikh congregation, and the formidable hilltop fortress at Gwalior, a Mughal site used to confine politically sensitive prisoners. The narrative linking these places has become central to Sikh collective memory. Yet telling it responsibly requires three layers: the documented political context of Jahangir's reign, later Sikh narratives of imprisonment and release, and modern practices of remembrance.

DATED TIMELINE
1595 — Guru Hargobind is born, traditionally at Guru ki Wadali near Amritsar.
1604 — The Adi Granth is installed at Harmandir Sahib under Guru Arjan.
1605 — Jahangir succeeds Akbar as Mughal emperor.
1606 — Guru Arjan dies in Mughal custody in Lahore; Guru Hargobind becomes sixth Guru.
c. 1606–1609 — Sikh tradition places the public assertion of Miri-Piri and establishment of the Akal Takht in the early Guruship; precise ceremony dates vary.
During Jahangir's reign (1605–1627) — Sikh histories place Guru Hargobind's confinement at Gwalior; proposed years and length of detention differ widely.
Release, date disputed — The Bandi Chhor narrative remembers the Guru departing with other captives.
1627 — Jahangir dies.
1628 — Shah Jahan becomes emperor; later armed encounters of Guru Hargobind's period are principally associated with his reign.
1644 — Guru Hargobind dies at Kiratpur; Guru Har Rai succeeds him.

1. THE POLITICAL SETTING
The fifth Guru's death in 1606 was not a minor local dispute. Jahangir's own memoir, the Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri, records hostility toward Guru Arjan's following and his order to punish him after the rebel prince Khusrau's visit. The sixth Guru inherited the memory of that intervention. He continued the Sikh religious tradition while adopting the visible signs of temporal leadership: armed attendants, horsemanship and the Akal Takht. Those developments could draw imperial attention, but they do not prove a single specific cause for the Gwalior detention.

Jahangir ruled a vast empire in which forts served as military installations and sites of detention for princes, nobles and other politically significant figures. Gwalior was such a site. The fact that a fortress was used for political prisoners helps explain the plausibility of the imprisonment tradition; it does not by itself verify the date, sentence, duration or names of fellow detainees.

2. WHAT CAN WE SAY ABOUT THE DETENTION?
Sikh historical literature consistently associates Guru Hargobind with detention at Gwalior and subsequent release. Accounts disagree on whether the detention resulted from concerns about the Guru's growing armed following, unresolved matters linked to Guru Arjan, financial claims or a combination of circumstances. Some later retellings offer a definite year and a precise number of months or years; these should not be mistaken for universally accepted contemporary documentation. There is no equivalent to Jahangir's explicit memoir passage on Guru Arjan that settles every detail of Guru Hargobind's Gwalior confinement.

The historical method matters: an account repeated in many modern pamphlets may still derive from a small number of later narratives. Repetition is not independent corroboration. Historians compare the age and provenance of sources, what each author could have known, and whether separate witnesses confirm the same claim.

3. THE RELEASE AND ITS MEANING
In the familiar Bandi Chhor account, the emperor agrees to release Guru Hargobind, who asks that imprisoned rulers also be allowed to leave. A famous version describes a garment with many trailing panels or tassels so that each prisoner could hold one while exiting. The number is commonly given as fifty-two. The story remembers a leader unwilling to accept freedom for himself alone. Yet the precise count, garment design, wording of the exchange and release date are not securely established by an independent contemporary court record. We can explain the narrative's religious meaning without pretending those details are verified archival facts.

4. BANDI CHHOR DIVAS AND DIWALI
Bandi Chhor Divas, literally the commemoration of the liberator of captives, is associated in Sikh tradition with Guru Hargobind's release and return. It is observed around the time of Diwali, and Amritsar's illumination is particularly famous. The relationship between the release narrative, the festival calendar and the historical practices of lighting at Harmandir Sahib has developed across time. The date of the modern annual observance should not be used as proof of the exact historical day the Guru left Gwalior. Likewise, the popular claim that all aspects of the modern festival began on one specific day in the seventeenth century goes beyond the available evidence.

5. AMRITSAR, GWALIOR AND KIRATPUR
Three places help orient this episode. Amritsar was the Sikh religious centre, with Harmandir Sahib and the Akal Takht symbolising distinct but related dimensions of the Guru's authority. Gwalior Fort, in present-day Madhya Pradesh, is the remembered site of imprisonment and liberation; Gurdwara Data Bandi Chhor commemorates the association. Kiratpur, in present-day Punjab, became an important later centre of Guru Hargobind's life. Geography reminds us that the sixth Guru's activity was not confined to a single settlement.

6. WHAT THE STORY DOES NOT MEAN
Bandi Chhor should not be used to claim that the Sikh Panth had already become the Khalsa; Guru Gobind Singh established the Khalsa in 1699. Nor does the story prove that every relationship between Sikhs and Mughal officials was hostile. Guru Hargobind's lifetime included confrontation, negotiation and periods remembered as accommodation. The major battles usually associated with the sixth Guru belong to the reign of Shah Jahan after 1628, not to the Gwalior story itself.

7. SCRIPTURE AND HISTORICAL ATTRIBUTION
Guru Hargobind is not assigned a body of hymns under a 'Mahalla 6' heading in the standard Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji. We should therefore not invent a quotation from him or attach an Ang number to a supposed Gwalior speech. The sixth Guru's legacy in this lesson is studied through historical narrative, institutions and later remembrance, while the scriptural continuity comes through the Gurbani preserved by his predecessors. For primary Gurbani already studied, Guru Arjan's 'ਤੇਰਾ ਕੀਆ ਮੀਠਾ ਲਾਗੈ' occurs on Ang 394 (Asa, Mahalla 5); it is not a quotation from Guru Hargobind or a transcript of events at Gwalior.

8. HOW TO READ THE SOURCES
For the wider history of the sixth Guruship, consult J. S. Grewal, The Sikhs of the Punjab, the section on the seventeenth-century Panth, and Khushwant Singh, A History of the Sikhs, volume I, the discussion of Guru Hargobind. For the devotional account of Bandi Chhor, compare the Encyclopaedia of Sikhism's entries on Guru Hargobind and Bandi Chhor with SGPC and Basics of Sikhi materials. The latter communicate the tradition but should not be treated as contemporary seventeenth-century witness statements. Source disagreement is not a reason to discard the episode; it is a reason to label each claim carefully.

The key historical lesson is that Guru Hargobind's remembered release became a durable expression of collective freedom and responsibility, while the historian must remain modest about precise dates and dramatic narrative details.

ATTRIBUTED SAKHI — THE FIFTY-TWO CAPTIVES
Later Sikh tradition, preserved in Sikh biographical and historical retellings and repeated in SGPC and Basics of Sikhi teaching, says that Guru Hargobind declined to leave Gwalior without other detained rulers. In a popular version, a robe was prepared with fifty-two extensions so that the prisoners could accompany him out. This is the basis of the widely taught Bandi Chhor account. Its message concerns the freedom of others, but the number fifty-two, robe, dialogue and precise date are details of the transmitted tradition rather than independently verified contemporary court evidence. No verbatim words are attributed to the Guru here.

EVIDENCE LADDER
Documented political context: Jahangir ruled 1605–1627; Guru Arjan died in 1606; Guru Hargobind succeeded him and later developed visible temporal leadership.
Strong Sikh historical tradition: Guru Hargobind's Gwalior detention and release.
Traditional details requiring qualification: fifty-two rulers, specially made robe, exact conversations and the duration or date of confinement.
Modern observance: Bandi Chhor Divas commemorates the release and is observed around Diwali; festival date is not a dated seventeenth-century prison register.

The Akal Takht and Miri-Piri provide the wider context of his leadership; the major Sikh–Mughal battles of the 1630s belong to the next stage under Shah Jahan. title: Guru Hargobind Ji: Battles under Shah Jahan and the Road to Kiratpur
period: 1628–1644 CE (battle dates and sequences vary across sources)
era: Sixth Guru — armed encounters and Kiratpur
intro: LESSON 22 | Thursday, 5 November 2026 | Morning | 8–10 minutes. After the Gwalior detention and Bandi Chhor tradition examined in Lesson 21, we turn to the reign of Shah Jahan and Guru Hargobind's armed encounters. Central question: How did a Sikh community organised around Gurbani, sangat and the Akal Takht respond to military confrontation, and why did Kiratpur become important? Guru Hargobind (1595–1644) succeeded Guru Arjan in 1606. Miri-Piri and the Akal Takht marked visible temporal authority, but the battles generally placed in the early 1630s belong to a later phase. This lesson distinguishes a credible broad pattern of fighting from exact battlefield numbers and dramatic episodes found in later narrative sources.
record:
DATED TIMELINE
1606 — Guru Arjan dies in Mughal custody; Guru Hargobind becomes sixth Guru.
c. 1609 — Traditional date associated with the Akal Takht in Amritsar.
1627 — Jahangir dies.
1628 — Shah Jahan takes the Mughal throne.
c. 1628–1635 — Sikh traditions and later histories place several confrontations involving Guru Hargobind and Mughal forces in this period; the exact year of individual engagements varies.
c. 1634 — Battle near Amritsar is commonly dated to this year in modern Sikh histories.

1. THE POLITICAL CHANGE IN 1628
Under Jahangir, Guru Hargobind's relations with the imperial court had included detention and, in some traditions, later accommodation. The accession of Shah Jahan in 1628 changed the court's political environment. Shah Jahan ruled a vast, resource-rich empire; his officials could mobilise armed contingents in Punjab. It is tempting to reduce the ensuing conflicts to an inevitable religious war, but the accounts mention specific disputes, including hunting, horses, local authority and rival claimants. The wider issue was the position of an increasingly autonomous religious community with its own leadership and armed retainers within an imperial province. The precise motives of individual Mughal commanders cannot always be recovered.

2. WHAT KIND OF ARMED COMMUNITY DID THE GURU LEAD?
Guru Hargobind had encouraged horsemanship, physical preparation and the maintenance of armed followers. This did not replace the sangat, langar or the centrality of Gurbani. It added a capacity for defence and public action. Cavalry needed animals, fodder, saddles, weapons, training and money. A permanent religious centre such as Amritsar, together with regional congregational networks, made organised support possible. But later claims about exact troop strengths and casualty counts should not be repeated as if they were verified muster rolls. There was no Khalsa institution yet: Guru Gobind Singh's Khalsa belongs to 1699, several generations later.

3. THE AMRITSAR CONFRONTATION
A battle near Amritsar, commonly dated 1634, is one of the best-known encounters. Sikh traditions frequently connect its outbreak with an incident involving a royal hunting party and a hawk or falcon. Some versions say the hawk was taken by the Guru's followers; others frame the dispute differently. The story gives a vivid immediate cause, but its details come through later narratives. Historians are more confident about a period of armed confrontation between the Guru's followers and Mughal forces than about the precise dialogue surrounding the bird. Accounts identify Sikh commanders and fighters, but lists vary. The fighting should be situated in the local political geography: Amritsar was not merely a shrine; it was a town, a market and a focal point of Sikh community organisation. A military encounter near it would have had implications for residents and travellers as well as armed men.

4. HARGOBINDPUR, MEHRAJ AND LAHIRA
The Guru's association with Hargobindpur on the Beas and the countryside of central Punjab forms part of the same wider history. Some narratives describe an earlier dispute at Hargobindpur involving local landholding and Mughal officials; historians differ on where to place that encounter in the sequence. Another battle is remembered near Lahira or Mehraj in the Malwa region, sometimes associated with the recovery of horses. The horse story illustrates the value of cavalry resources but should be read as a traditional explanation rather than a contemporaneous military dispatch. The dates and sequence of these battles vary between historical works. A responsible chronological account records the cluster of conflicts in the early-to-mid 1630s without asserting that every episode can be assigned to an exact day.

5. KARTARPUR AND PAINDE KHAN
A later confrontation is traditionally placed at Kartarpur near Jalandhar — not Guru Nanak's Kartarpur on the Ravi, now in Pakistan. Sikh narratives prominently feature Painde Khan, once associated with Guru Hargobind's household and later remembered as an opponent. Dramatic descriptions of personal combat between the Guru and Painde Khan occur in later historical literature. They are important to the tradition but should not be presented as independently verified transcripts or precise eyewitness reports. The broader account points to changing loyalties and the political complexity of Punjab: relationships were not determined simply by whether someone was Sikh or Muslim. Later sources disagree on the exact date and circumstances of this battle, often assigning it to about 1634 or 1635.

6. WHY KIRATPUR MATTERED
Kiratpur lies in the foothill region of present-day Rupnagar district, Punjab, near the Shivalik hills. Sikh tradition associates its establishment with Baba Gurditta, Guru Hargobind's son, and with the Guru's later residence. The settlement offered a different setting from the busy imperial plains around Lahore and Amritsar. It became a major centre for the Guru's family and Sikh congregations. Explaining the move solely as a military retreat would be too simple: geography, community networks, family connections and religious activity also mattered. Guru Hargobind spent his final years there and died in 1644. Kiratpur remained important under later Gurus, including Guru Har Rai and Guru Har Krishan, and is closely connected to the early life of Guru Tegh Bahadur.

7. THE SUCCESSION TO GURU HAR RAI
Guru Hargobind's successor was his grandson Guru Har Rai, traditionally born in 1630. Guru Har Rai became the seventh Guru in 1644. The succession demonstrates that Sikh leadership continued through family relationships but was not reducible to automatic inheritance by the eldest son. The sixth Guru's career left a community with established scriptural worship, institutions of public authority, regional settlements and experience of armed conflict. Yet the next Guru's leadership would develop under its own circumstances and should not be treated as an uninterrupted continuation of battlefield campaigning.

8. READING THE SOURCES CRITICALLY
For the early seventeenth century, historians compare Sikh literary traditions with Persian court histories and later historical compilations. J. S. Grewal, The Sikhs of the Punjab, sections on the Sikh Panth under the sixth Guru, offers a concise scholarly synthesis. Khushwant Singh, A History of the Sikhs, Volume I, the section on Guru Hargobind, narrates the confrontations but also reflects the limits of the surviving record. The Encyclopaedia of Sikhism (Punjabi University) offers entries for Guru Hargobind, Hargobindpur, Kiratpur and Painde Khan. Basics of Sikhi/WhyGuru presents the devotional Sikh understanding; it is valuable for tradition, but should not replace source criticism. The Gurus' scriptural teaching remained central, but there is no authenticated Mahalla 6 composition in the standard Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji: no invented quotation or ang number should be attributed to Guru Hargobind. Earlier Gurbani such as Guru Nanak's criticism of political violence (Asa ki Var, Ang 360) supplies wider ethical context, not a verbatim explanation of any 1630s battle.

KEY PEOPLE AND PLACES
Guru Hargobind — sixth Guru; Shah Jahan — Mughal emperor from 1628; Baba Gurditta — son of Guru Hargobind, associated with Kiratpur; Painde Khan — figure in Kartarpur battle traditions; Guru Har Rai — seventh Guru from 1644. Amritsar — major Sikh centre; Hargobindpur — settlement near the Beas; Mehraj/Lahira — Malwa battle traditions; Kartarpur near Jalandhar — site associated with a later confrontation; Kiratpur — foothill centre of the Guru's later years.

SOURCE-BASED TRADITION — THE HAWK AND THE AMRITSAR BATTLE

The incident supposedly escalated into armed conflict near Amritsar. This is a traditional explanation of the immediate trigger, not an independently documented imperial hunting report. The existence of a broader pattern of armed encounters is more secure than the precise hawk episode, speeches, combat numbers or exact sequence. Another popular tradition describes Guru Hargobind personally defeating Painde Khan at Kartarpur. That account also needs explicit attribution to later narrative literature. Neither story should be turned into a fabricated quotation from the Guru.

Exact dates, numbers and colourful incidents differ between sources. Guru Hargobind's organisation combined continuing religious institutions with armed self-defence, not the later Khalsa of 1699. Kiratpur became a major centre of his later life; he died there in 1644, and Guru Har Rai succeeded him. title: Guru Har Rai Ji: Kiratpur, Compassion and the Mughal Succession Crisis
intro:
LESSON 23 — GURU HAR RAI JI: KIRATPUR, COMPASSION AND THE MUGHAL SUCCESSION CRISIS
Thursday, 5 November 2026 | Evening | 8–10 minute reading

CENTRAL QUESTION: How did Guru Har Rai preserve the Sikh Panth's religious and defensive institutions while navigating a succession struggle at the Mughal court?

Guru Hargobind died at Kiratpur in 1644 after a Guruship marked by the Akal Takht, Miri-Piri and armed confrontations under Shah Jahan. His grandson Guru Har Rai, then approximately fourteen, succeeded him. The seventh Guru's life is often reduced to stories of flowers, healing and kindness. These traditions are meaningful, but they should be set alongside the political reality of seventeenth-century Punjab. Guru Har Rai inherited an established Sikh congregation, regional networks and an armed following. His Guruship was generally less openly confrontational than his grandfather's, yet the imperial succession crisis of 1657–1659 brought the Sikh centre into the orbit of Mughal politics.

DATED TIMELINE
• 16 January 1630 (traditional date): Har Rai born, generally placed at Kiratpur; son of Baba Gurditta and Mata Nihal Kaur, grandson of Guru Hargobind.
• 1644: Guru Hargobind dies; Har Rai becomes seventh Guru at Kiratpur.
• 1657: Shah Jahan becomes seriously ill; his sons compete for succession.
• 1658: Dara Shikoh loses the struggle to Aurangzeb, who takes power.
• 1659: Dara is captured and executed; later narratives connect him to Guru Har Rai's aid.
• 1661: Guru Har Rai dies at Kiratpur; his younger son Har Krishan succeeds him. Dates for some individual encounters differ among historical accounts.

PEOPLE AND PLACES: Guru Har Rai (seventh Guru); Baba Gurditta (his father); Guru Hargobind (grandfather); Mata Nihal Kaur (mother); Ram Rai and Har Krishan (sons); Dara Shikoh (Shah Jahan's eldest son and Aurangzeb's rival); Aurangzeb (Mughal emperor from 1658); Kiratpur Sahib (Shivalik foothill centre); Delhi (imperial court); Punjab (heartland of Sikh congregations).
record:
1. KIRATPUR AND CONTINUITY
Kiratpur Sahib, in the foothill region of present-day Rupnagar district, had grown in importance during Guru Hargobind's later years. The seventh Guru's succession did not mean that the community abandoned Miri-Piri or the ability to defend itself. Sikh histories describe Guru Har Rai maintaining an armed body of retainers, often conventionally numbered at 2,200 horsemen; this number is traditional and should not be mistaken for a surviving contemporary muster roll. The crucial historical point is continuity of an organised community alongside a period of relatively limited direct warfare. The Guru's residence remained a centre for visitors, religious instruction, and service. Amritsar and other earlier Sikh centres retained their historical importance.

2. COMPASSION AS A PRACTICAL ETHIC
Guru Har Rai is especially remembered for concern for living creatures and medicinal plants. Later Sikh narratives describe him cultivating a garden and dispensary and using medicinal resources to assist the sick. These accounts express a model of seva (service) that includes care rather than only ritual observance. The precise layout of the garden, its inventory and individual medical treatments are not securely reconstructed from contemporary records. A historian can acknowledge the importance of the remembered tradition without claiming that a particular herbal prescription is independently verified.

The ethical theme fits wider Sikh teachings, but we should not invent a 'Mahalla 7' quotation: no compositions attributed to Guru Har Rai under that heading occur in the standard Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji. One relevant earlier scriptural line is Guru Nanak's 'ਪਵਣੁ ਗੁਰੂ ਪਾਣੀ ਪਿਤਾ ਮਾਤਾ ਧਰਤਿ ਮਹਤੁ ॥' (Japji Sahib, Ang 8): air is guru, water father, and earth the great mother. This verse offers broader context for reflection on living in the world, not a direct eyewitness description of Guru Har Rai's garden. Another line, 'ਸਭਨਾ ਜੀਆ ਕਾ ਇਕੁ ਦਾਤਾ ਸੋ ਮੈ ਵਿਸਰਿ ਨ ਜਾਈ ॥' (Japji Sahib, Ang 2), identifies the one giver of all beings. Its Ang attribution should be checked in the original text; neither line is a newly composed teaching of the seventh Guru.

3. DARA SHIKOH AND THE MUGHAL COURT
Shah Jahan's eldest son Dara Shikoh was associated with intellectual interest in Sufi thought and translations of Indian religious texts. When Shah Jahan became ill in 1657, rival princes competed for power. Aurangzeb defeated Dara's forces in 1658 and ultimately took the throne. Dara was executed in 1659. Sikh tradition connects Guru Har Rai with helping Dara, sometimes describing the provision of medicinal assistance and, in other accounts, support during his flight. Versions differ on the timing and nature of the help. These details should not be collapsed into a single securely documented court episode. What is historically secure is the Mughal succession struggle and its outcome; the exact character of Guru Har Rai's assistance is preserved mainly through Sikh narrative sources.

Why would a Sikh leader become involved? Guru Har Rai presided over a community with regional influence and resources. Offering aid to a sick or endangered person could reflect compassion; imperial authorities might nevertheless interpret assistance to a defeated prince politically. This tension is important for understanding how religious service and state power intersected.

4. RAM RAI AT AURANGZEB'S COURT
A well-known Sikh traditional account says Aurangzeb summoned Guru Har Rai to explain a line of Gurbani. The Guru sent his elder son Ram Rai instead. At court, Ram Rai is said to have altered the wording of a verse to avoid offending the emperor. The traditionally cited text is 'ਮਿਟੀ ਮੁਸਲਮਾਨ ਕੀ ਪੇੜੈ ਪਈ ਕੁਮ੍ਹ੍ਹਿਆਰ ॥' from Guru Nanak's Asa ki Var, Ang 466; it forms part of a longer passage that must be read in context. Later narratives say Ram Rai replaced 'ਮੁਸਲਮਾਨ' with 'ਬੇਈਮਾਨ' in his explanation. The story illustrates the principle that Gurbani must not be changed to please a ruler. The specific court dialogue, however, comes from later Sikh accounts, not a surviving verbatim Mughal transcript. Ram Rai later became associated with Dehradun and a distinct following.

The broader lesson is not that one should read a single line without context: Guru Nanak's verse addresses death, material existence and religious assumptions. Interpretation requires the surrounding stanza and original language. For exact scriptural reading, consult Ang 466 rather than relying on a paraphrase of the court anecdote.

5. SUCCESSION IN 1661
Guru Har Rai chose his younger son Har Krishan as successor rather than Ram Rai. Sikh tradition links this choice to the episode at court and Ram Rai's alteration of Gurbani. The seventh Guru died in 1661 at Kiratpur, and Guru Har Krishan became the eighth Guru while still a child. This succession shows that the Guruship was not simply automatic inheritance by the eldest son. It also introduced a new period of tension involving the imperial court, which we will study in the next lesson.

6. HISTORICAL INTERPRETATION
J. S. Grewal's The Sikhs of the Punjab places this Guruship within the continued growth of Sikh institutions and Mughal relations; Khushwant Singh's A History of the Sikhs, volume I, provides another narrative account. These works should be read alongside the Punjabi University Encyclopaedia of Sikhism and the traditional teaching of Basics of Sikhi / WhyGuru. Neither scholarly overview should be cited as a source for invented direct speech. For the succession war, the dates of Shah Jahan's illness, Aurangzeb's accession and Dara's defeat are better attested than the details of the medicinal-help sakhi.

WHY THIS PERIOD MATTERS
The seventh Guru's leadership was not a retreat from history. It illustrates how the Sikh Panth could preserve its institutions and capacity for defence while emphasising service, education and compassion. At the same time, the Mughal succession crisis demonstrated that even humanitarian or spiritual decisions could acquire political consequences. Kiratpur became a bridge between Guru Hargobind's martial legacy and the short Guruship of Guru Har Krishan.
tradition:
SAKHI — THE FLOWER AND THE ROBE (TRADITIONAL, NOT A CONTEMPORARY RECORD)
A popular story describes young Har Rai walking through a garden when his clothing brushed against flowers and damaged them. He is said to have learned to move more carefully so that he would not needlessly harm living things. The sakhi is used in Sikh teaching to illustrate sensitivity and compassion. Its dialogue and the exact circumstances are not independently documented in a seventeenth-century eyewitness source. It should be attributed to later Sikh oral and biographical tradition, not to the original Gurbani or to a verified Mughal court record.

A second commonly recounted sakhi describes Guru Har Rai providing medicines for Dara Shikoh. This, too, belongs to the Sikh historical tradition; its exact prescription and dates cannot be securely verified. These accounts should be appreciated as teachings about seva while keeping their evidentiary status clear.
recap: RECAP — Guru Har Rai (1630–1661), grandson of Guru Hargobind, became seventh Guru in 1644 at Kiratpur. His leadership maintained Sikh community organisation and a defensive following while being especially remembered for compassion and care. The Mughal succession struggle of 1657–1659 brought Dara Shikoh and Aurangzeb into the historical picture; traditional accounts of the Guru's assistance to Dara are not independently established in every detail. Ram Rai's reported alteration of a Gurbani line at court is a traditional explanation for the succession of the younger Har Krishan in 1661. Gurbani attributed to Guru Nanak, not Guru Har Rai, appears on Angs 2, 8 and 466 in the passages discussed. NEXT — Lesson 24: Guru Har Krishan Ji, Delhi, the smallpox tradition and succession in 1664.

title: Guru Har Krishan Ji: Delhi, Service and the Succession of 1664
intro:
LESSON 24 | Friday, 6 November 2026 | Morning | Approximately 8–10 minutes.

CENTRAL QUESTION: How did a child become the eighth Sikh Guru, why is his short life remembered for service in Delhi, and what do the sources actually establish?

Guru Har Krishan Ji succeeded his father Guru Har Rai in 1661, when he was about five. This followed a period of Mughal political instability and the dispute involving his elder brother Ram Rai. The eighth Guru's Guruship lasted less than three years. Sikh tradition remembers his compassion during illness in Delhi, the site now commemorated by Gurdwara Bangla Sahib, and the final indication 'Baba Bakale' pointing toward the next Guru. We will distinguish the established succession and death in 1664 from later detailed sakhis about miracles and the epidemic.
record:
DATED TIMELINE
7 July 1656 — Traditional birth date of Guru Har Krishan at Kiratpur Sahib, son of Guru Har Rai and Mata Krishan Kaur (also called Sulakhni in some sources).
1661 — Guru Har Rai dies at Kiratpur; Har Krishan succeeds as eighth Guru, approximately five years old.
1661–1664 — Dispute involving elder brother Ram Rai and competing claims to authority; Aurangzeb reigns at Delhi.
1664 — Guru Har Krishan travels to Delhi, traditionally at the invitation or through the mediation of Raja Jai Singh; exact details of the summons vary.
30 March 1664 — Commonly accepted traditional date of Guru Har Krishan's death in Delhi, aged seven; smallpox is the illness most often named in Sikh histories.
1664 — Guru Tegh Bahadur, based at Bakala, becomes ninth Guru; the recognition process and rival claims require separate treatment in the next lesson.

1. A CHILD AS GURU
Guru Har Krishan was the younger son of Guru Har Rai and grandson of Baba Gurditta. His great-grandfather was Guru Hargobind. His accession at roughly five years of age challenges the assumption that the Sikh Guruship depended on age, seniority or military experience. The institution was understood by Sikhs as the continuation of the Guru's spiritual authority. The earlier succession to Guru Angad rather than Guru Nanak's sons, and to Guru Arjan rather than his older brothers, had already demonstrated that succession was not automatic primogeniture. The eighth Guru inherited established congregational networks, the teachings preserved in the Adi Granth and the religious centre at Kiratpur.

2. THE RAM RAI DISPUTE
The previous lesson examined the traditional story of Ram Rai's appearance at Aurangzeb's court. According to Sikh accounts, he altered a word of Guru Nanak's Gurbani while explaining it, in order to appease the emperor. Guru Har Rai instead appointed his younger son. Ram Rai later developed his own following and is associated with Dehradun. The specific court conversation is preserved in later Sikh narrative traditions, not a verbatim surviving court transcript. Its significance within Sikh memory is the principle that Gurbani should not be altered for political favour. The relevant original line appears in Asa ki Var, Guru Nanak, Ang 466; it must be read in the context of the complete stanza.

3. WHY DELHI MATTERED
Delhi was the imperial centre of Aurangzeb's Mughal state. The growing Sikh Panth could not entirely avoid court politics, especially while rival claims to the Guruship existed. Traditional histories connect Guru Har Krishan's journey to Delhi with Raja Jai Singh of Amber, a powerful Mughal noble. Some accounts describe a summons from Aurangzeb; others emphasise Jai Singh's invitation or mediation. We should not flatten these versions into a single independently verified dialogue. Delhi's political setting helps explain why the young Guru's visit mattered beyond the city itself.

4. RAJA JAI SINGH'S HOUSE AND BANGLA SAHIB
Sikh tradition places the Guru at the residence of Raja Jai Singh in Delhi. The site is commemorated today by Gurdwara Bangla Sahib. The modern gurdwara and its sarovar are later architectural and institutional developments, not unchanged seventeenth-century structures. The remembered association with the Guru is historically significant, but a visitor should distinguish the site of commemoration from direct physical remains of the original lodging. The Guru's brief Delhi stay is central to Sikh remembrance of his care for the suffering.

5. EPIDEMIC, WATER AND SERVICE
The Guru's death is commonly attributed to smallpox. Sikh traditions describe a devastating outbreak of disease in Delhi and the young Guru tending people regardless of social status. Some narratives say he provided water or blessed a source of water associated with healing. The details of individual cures and the precise scale and diagnosis of the epidemic are not independently established by a contemporary medical register. It is therefore more accurate to say that Sikh tradition remembers compassionate service during widespread illness, while the death of the Guru in Delhi in 1664 is part of the accepted historical chronology. The popular epithet 'Bala Pir' (child saint) expresses reverence for his youthful spiritual leadership. Do not mistake a miraculous healing story for a clinical finding or medical recommendation.

6. SAKHI: THE SCHOLAR AND THE WATER-CARRIER
A widely retold Sikh sakhi says that on the route to Delhi, a learned Brahmin named Lal Chand challenged the young Guru's understanding of the Bhagavad Gita. Guru Har Krishan asked an unlettered water-carrier, often called Chhajju, to explain its meaning. In the story the humble labourer speaks with surprising insight, overturning pride in social rank and formal learning. Versions differ in names, location, and dialogue; this is a later traditional narrative, not an independently authenticated transcript. Its teaching is that spiritual wisdom cannot be monopolised by caste or educational status. The story should not be quoted as a historical stenographic record.

7. THE FINAL WORDS: 'BABA BAKALE'
According to Sikh tradition, before dying the young Guru indicated 'Baba Bakale', pointing the community toward Bakala, a settlement associated with Guru Tegh Bahadur. The phrase is transmitted in later narratives, and the precise words and ceremony are not established by contemporary eyewitness documentation. The succession was not instantly uncontested: several claimants emerged, and the story of Makhan Shah Lubana's recognition of Guru Tegh Bahadur belongs to the next stage. Guru Har Krishan died in Delhi in 1664, aged seven; the shrine Gurdwara Bala Sahib commemorates the place associated with his cremation.

8. WHAT GURBANI CAN AND CANNOT TELL US
There are no compositions headed 'Mahalla 8' in the standard Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji, so it would be false to invent a verse or ang attributed to Guru Har Krishan. A relevant earlier teaching appears in Guru Nanak's Japji Sahib, Ang 2: 'ਸਭਨਾ ਜੀਆ ਕਾ ਇਕੁ ਦਾਤਾ ਸੋ ਮੈ ਵਿਸਰਿ ਨ ਜਾਈ ॥' — there is one giver to all beings; may I not forget that One. This is a theological connection to service, not a record of an incident in Delhi. The original Gurbani is primary textual evidence; the sakhi literature is a different genre with different historical evidentiary limits.

9. THE BROADER HISTORICAL SIGNIFICANCE
Guru Har Krishan's short Guruship links the relatively settled Kiratpur period of Guru Har Rai to the more difficult political and religious circumstances of Guru Tegh Bahadur. His life is remembered for humility, service and compassion rather than battles or monumental construction. The continuation of Guruship through a child also reveals that Sikh authority was understood as spiritual and institutional, not simply the personal power of an adult commander. Later commemorative traditions at Bangla Sahib and Bala Sahib show how Delhi became an enduring part of Sikh sacred geography.

KEY PEOPLE AND PLACES
Guru Har Krishan — eighth Guru, 1656–1664; Guru Har Rai — father and seventh Guru; Mata Krishan Kaur — mother; Ram Rai — elder brother and rival claimant; Aurangzeb — Mughal emperor; Raja Jai Singh — noble associated with the Guru's Delhi stay; Guru Tegh Bahadur — successor; Kiratpur — early home and accession; Delhi — final visit and death; Bangla Sahib — commemorative site of lodging and service; Bala Sahib — commemorative site associated with cremation; Bakala — associated with the next Guru.
tradition:
ATTRIBUTED SAKHI — CHHAJJU THE WATER-CARRIER
Later Sikh biographical tradition tells of a proud scholar, often called Lal Chand, who challenged the child Guru. Guru Har Krishan is said to have enabled Chhajju, a humble water-carrier, to explain a difficult sacred text. The account illustrates the Sikh rejection of spiritual pride based on caste and formal learning. Details vary between retellings, and the miraculous exchange is not supported by a contemporary eyewitness transcript. It should be taught as a traditional sakhi, not as independently established courtroom-style testimony.

A second tradition connects the Guru's stay at Raja Jai Singh's Delhi residence with compassionate care during an epidemic. The historic association is commemorated at Bangla Sahib; specific miraculous cures remain devotional tradition.
recap: RECAP — Guru Har Krishan (1656–1664) became eighth Guru in 1661 at about five years old, after Guru Har Rai selected him over Ram Rai. He visited Delhi during Aurangzeb's reign, where tradition places him at Raja Jai Singh's residence and remembers his service during an outbreak of illness. He died in Delhi in 1664, traditionally of smallpox. Bangla Sahib and Bala Sahib commemorate his stay and death. The Chhajju sakhi and 'Baba Bakale' final indication are later traditional accounts whose precise dialogue cannot be independently verified. No Mahalla 8 Gurbani exists in the standard scripture. title: Guru Tegh Bahadur Ji: Baba Bakala, Makhan Shah Lubana and the Ninth Guruship
intro:
LESSON 25 — GURU TEGH BAHADUR JI: BABA BAKALA AND THE NINTH GURUSHIP
Friday, 6 November 2026 | Evening | Approximately 9 minutes

CENTRAL QUESTION: How did the Sikh community identify its ninth Guru after the death of seven-year-old Guru Har Krishan, and what can we distinguish between early evidence and later stories?

The eighth Guru, Guru Har Krishan, died in Delhi in 1664. Sikh tradition remembers his final indication as “Baba Bakale,” directing followers toward Bakala in Punjab. The community was now navigating an unusually difficult succession: its previous Guru had been a child, Ram Rai maintained a rival following, and multiple people at Bakala reportedly claimed authority. Guru Tegh Bahadur, the youngest son of Guru Hargobind and uncle of Guru Har Krishan's father Guru Har Rai, eventually emerged as the ninth Guru. His early leadership preceded the founding of Chak Nanaki, later associated with Anandpur Sahib, and the extensive travels that will form our next lesson.

DATED TIMELINE
• 1 April 1621 (traditional date): Tegh Bahadur born at Amritsar to Guru Hargobind and Mata Nanaki.
• 1630s: Traditions associate him with Guru Hargobind's martial training and the Battle of Kartarpur; precise battlefield details are later narratives.
• 1633 (traditional date): Marriage to Mata Gujri.
• 1644: Guru Hargobind dies; Guru Har Rai succeeds; Tegh Bahadur lives for an extended period in Bakala.
• March 1664: Guru Har Krishan dies at Delhi; Sikh tradition remembers the words “Baba Bakale.”
• 1664: Recognition of Guru Tegh Bahadur at Bakala; Makhan Shah Lubana's identification belongs to the well-known traditional account.
• 1665: Guru Tegh Bahadur's early travels and establishment of Chak Nanaki in the foothills, subsequently linked to Anandpur Sahib.

PEOPLE AND PLACES: Guru Tegh Bahadur (ninth Guru); Guru Hargobind (his father); Mata Nanaki (mother); Mata Gujri (wife); Guru Har Krishan (eighth Guru); Makhan Shah Lubana (merchant in succession tradition); Dhir Mal (a rival claimant in later narratives); Bakala, Amritsar, Kiratpur, and Chak Nanaki (important places).
record:
1. THE FAMILY CONNECTION
Guru Tegh Bahadur was born Tyag Mal, according to common Sikh biographical tradition, in 1621. His father Guru Hargobind had combined the community's religious institutions with a more visible capacity for defence. Traditional accounts say that Tyag Mal received the name Tegh Bahadur (“brave with the sword”) for courage during conflict, often linked to Kartarpur. The precise naming episode is a later biographical tradition, not a contemporary military citation. He married Mata Gujri; their son, the future Guru Gobind Singh, would be born in 1666.

2. LIFE AT BAKALA
Bakala, in the Amritsar region, was associated with Tegh Bahadur's extended residence and religious discipline. Accounts often portray him as spending many years in meditation, but this should not be misread as evidence that he was wholly absent from family or communal life. The Sikh community already had established networks of sangat, religious instruction, and movement between towns. Guru Tegh Bahadur's later travels demonstrate that the ninth Guruship did not remain confined to Bakala.

3. THE SUCCESSION PROBLEM OF 1664
Guru Har Krishan died at Delhi in March 1664. His short Guruship had already involved a contested claim from his elder brother Ram Rai. The words “Baba Bakale” are reported in later Sikh tradition as the dying Guru's indication of the next centre of succession. They do not appear as a recorded final declaration in the Guru Granth Sahib, and no contemporary verbatim transcript survives. The story nevertheless explains why Bakala became the focus of the search for a successor.

Later Sikh narratives speak of numerous claimants at Bakala, sometimes numbering twenty-two. The number and the individual claimants' identities vary among sources. Dhir Mal, a descendant of Guru Hargobind through Baba Gurditta, appears in traditions of competing authority. A historian should distinguish the broad existence of succession disputes from the exact theatrical detail of every later retelling.

4. THE RECOGNITION OF THE NINTH GURU
Guru Tegh Bahadur came to be recognised by the principal Sikh community as ninth Guru in 1664. Recognition required more than one traveller's statement: the established Sikh congregations, family connections, devotional authority, and continuing networks of followers all mattered. The popular Makhan Shah narrative expresses this process through a memorable episode, but its miraculous or private details cannot be independently confirmed. Later histories also tell of opposition and an attack associated with Dhir Mal's faction; the details should be treated cautiously.

5. WHAT DID THE NINTH GURU TEACH?
Guru Tegh Bahadur's bani is preserved in Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji, unlike the eighth Guru, to whom no separate Mahalla 8 compositions are assigned. One verified example is the salok beginning “ਜੋ ਨਰੁ ਦੁਖ ਮੈ ਦੁਖੁ ਨਹੀ ਮਾਨੈ ॥” on Ang 1427, attributed to Mahalla 9. It describes spiritual steadiness amid suffering, pleasure, praise, blame, fear, and attachment. Its theme is not emotional indifference toward others; rather, it concerns freedom from domination by changing circumstances. The line is scriptural evidence of the ninth Guru's teaching, not a contemporary description of the Makhan Shah episode. The ninth Guru's saloks appear near the end of the standard 1,430-Ang scripture, and his compositions occur elsewhere under raag headings. Always distinguish the later standard Ang pagination from the folio numbering of earlier manuscripts.

6. THE FIRST MOVEMENTS BEYOND BAKALA
The ninth Guru's early travels included visits to important Sikh centres and the foothill region. In 1665 the settlement of Chak Nanaki was established on land associated in tradition with a purchase from local hill rulers; it later developed into the Anandpur Sahib complex. Dates and the exact transaction differ in some accounts. This was a significant continuation of earlier Gurus' practice of developing settlements as religious and social centres. The next lesson will explore Chak Nanaki, the eastern travels, and the broader political landscape.

7. HISTORICAL METHOD
J. S. Grewal, The Sikhs of the Punjab, and Khushwant Singh, A History of the Sikhs, volume I, provide scholarly historical context for the transition from the eighth to ninth Guru. The Punjabi University Encyclopaedia of Sikhism offers biographical and place-based entries. Basics of Sikhi / WhyGuru explains the devotional meaning of the succession traditions. None of these should be treated as furnishing a contemporary stenographic record of Makhan Shah's exclamation or the precise number of claimants. For scripture consult Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji, Ang 1427, Mahalla 9, using the original Gurmukhi and a reliable commentary such as Professor Sahib Singh's Guru Granth Darpan.

WHY IT MATTERS
The succession of 1664 reveals both continuity and vulnerability in the early Sikh Panth. A community spanning many congregations had to identify religious leadership amid competing claims. Guru Tegh Bahadur's recognition set the stage for new settlements, travels across northern and eastern India, and ultimately the crisis of 1675. Those later events should not be projected backward onto every detail of the Bakala episode.
tradition:
SAKHI — MAKHAN SHAH LUBANA AND “GURU LADHO RE” (TRADITIONAL ACCOUNT)
A merchant named Makhan Shah Lubana, travelling by sea, is said to have prayed for rescue from danger and promised an offering of 500 gold coins to the Guru. After reaching Bakala, he reportedly tested several claimants by offering only a small amount. When he approached Guru Tegh Bahadur, the Guru is said to have reminded him of the full vow. Makhan Shah then proclaimed “Guru ladho re!” — “I have found the Guru!” This is a later Sikh sakhi, not an independently verified ship's log, financial record, or contemporary transcript. Its lesson is that spiritual authenticity cannot be established merely through public claims or outward display. The commonly repeated figures (500 coins and 22 claimants) belong to the narrative tradition and should be attributed as such.
recap:
RECAP: Guru Tegh Bahadur, born in 1621 and a son of Guru Hargobind, was recognised as ninth Guru in 1664 after Guru Har Krishan's death. Bakala became central to the succession tradition. Makhan Shah Lubana's story and the exclamation “Guru ladho re” convey the community's memory of recognition, but the private dialogue and exact numbers cannot be independently verified. The ninth Guru's own bani is preserved in Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji; Ang 1427 provides a powerful teaching about steadiness amid suffering. Chak Nanaki's establishment in 1665 prepared the way for the later development of Anandpur Sahib. NEXT: Guru Tegh Bahadur's travels and the founding of Chak Nanaki.

Source titles are reading recommendations, not claims that particular traditional dialogue is verified.

title: Guru Tegh Bahadur Ji: Chak Nanaki, Travels and the Expanding Sikh Panth
intro: Guru Tegh Bahadur Ji established Chak Nanaki in 1665 and travelled across northern and eastern India, strengthening Sikh congregational connections. His family was associated with Patna, where Gobind Rai was born in 1666.
record:
LESSON 26 — SATURDAY MORNING, 7 NOVEMBER 2026
GURU TEGH BAHADUR JI: CHAK NANAKI, TRAVELS AND THE EXPANDING SIKH PANTH
Period: 1664–1672 CE | Reading time: approximately 9 minutes

CENTRAL QUESTION
Why did the ninth Guru establish a new settlement near the Shivalik foothills and undertake journeys across northern and eastern India? What can we know about these travels without confusing later pilgrimage traditions with contemporary travel diaries?

1. THE CONTEXT AFTER BAKALA
In 1664, following the death of Guru Har Krishan Ji in Delhi, Guru Tegh Bahadur Ji was recognised as the ninth Guru. Our preceding lesson examined the contested succession at Bakala and the Makhan Shah Lubana sakhi. The Guru inherited a Panth with congregations spread beyond Punjab, but also with rival claims and the political uncertainty of Aurangzeb's reign. His response was not confined to a single religious centre: journeys, community contact and the development of a settlement became prominent features of his Guruship. We should distinguish the well-attested broader expansion of the Sikh network from individual speeches and miracles preserved in later narratives.

2. DATED TIMELINE
1621 — Guru Tegh Bahadur born in Amritsar (traditional birth chronology).
1664 — Recognised as ninth Guru following Guru Har Krishan's death.
1665 — Chak Nanaki founded near Makhowal in the Shivalik foothills; the site later developed into Anandpur Sahib.
1665–1666 — Journeys through parts of northern India; traditional itineraries include the region of Delhi, present-day Uttar Pradesh and Bihar.
22 December 1666 — Birth of Gobind Rai (later Guru Gobind Singh) at Patna, while Guru Tegh Bahadur was travelling elsewhere; the exact stages of the Guru's route vary by account.
Late 1660s–early 1670s — Traditions associate the Guru with congregations in Bihar, Bengal and Assam, as well as subsequent return journeys.
1675 — The ninth Guru's execution in Delhi; this event belongs to a later lesson and must not be used to explain every earlier decision retroactively.

3. CHAK NANAKI: A PLACE, NOT YET THE LATER ANANDPUR
In 1665, Guru Tegh Bahadur established a settlement called Chak Nanaki, honouring his mother Mata Nanaki. The site lay in the foothill region near Makhowal. Sikh histories associate its acquisition with land obtained from local hill authorities; the precise form and terms of the transaction differ among accounts. The settlement later became part of the historical development of Anandpur Sahib. It is anachronistic to imagine the entire eighteenth-century fortified Anandpur already existing in 1665. Those forts and the Khalsa's later history belong to Guru Gobind Singh's period.

Why establish a new centre? A town could house residents, accommodate travelling sangats, provide a place for religious gatherings and connect communities across routes between Punjab and the hills. The Sikh Gurus had repeatedly created or strengthened centres: Kartarpur under Guru Nanak, Goindwal under Guru Amar Das, Ramdaspur under Guru Ram Das and Amritsar under Guru Arjan. Chak Nanaki continued this pattern of institution-building. It also gave the ninth Guru's household and community a geographical base.

4. TRAVEL AS A FORM OF LEADERSHIP
Guru Tegh Bahadur's travels are remembered across an unusually wide region. Accounts connect him with communities in present-day Punjab, Haryana, Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Bengal and Assam. The routes and precise dates cannot all be reconstructed from surviving contemporary records. A gurdwara marking a visit demonstrates a living tradition of remembrance; it does not, on its own, prove the date, duration or exact speech of a seventeenth-century encounter.

The journeys matter because Sikh congregations were not limited to a single Punjab town. Long-distance traders, travellers, householders and local communities helped maintain religious connections. Visiting sangats could reinforce shared teachings, encourage service and create durable relationships. We should not assume a single modern itinerary or a uniformly documented travel schedule.

5. PATNA AND THE GURU'S FAMILY
Patna, an important city on the Ganges, became closely associated with the ninth Guru's family. Mata Gujri Ji was in Patna when Gobind Rai was born on 22 December 1666, according to the widely accepted Sikh chronology. Guru Tegh Bahadur was away travelling at the time. The city is commemorated today at Takht Sri Patna Sahib. The present shrine's architecture is much later than the birth event; the sacred association and the surviving building's construction history must be considered separately.

This period is important for two distinct reasons. First, it shows the geographic breadth of the Sikh community. Second, it links the life of the ninth Guru to the childhood of the future tenth Guru. The boy born at Patna would later establish the Khalsa in 1699, but that outcome should not be read as a predetermined plan documented in the 1660s.

6. EASTERN JOURNEYS AND ASSAM: WHAT IS CERTAIN?
Later Sikh sources associate Guru Tegh Bahadur with eastern journeys extending toward Bengal and Assam. Some narratives link his presence in the region with the Mughal commander Raja Ram Singh's expedition toward Assam. Historians debate the exact overlap, chronology and nature of any encounter. The expedition itself belongs to Mughal-Ahom political history; a specific personal meeting or intervention by the Guru requires its own evidence. Avoid repeating as fact claims that the Guru single-handedly brokered a peace treaty unless a source directly establishes it.

The wider setting is significant: eastern India had trade routes, military campaigns, pilgrimage networks and religious communities. A travelling Guru could encounter diverse populations. But modern commemorative geography is not equivalent to a complete seventeenth-century diary.

7. A SAKHI OF SERVICE — ATTRIBUTED TO LATER TRADITION
Traditional Sikh narratives about the ninth Guru's journeys frequently describe him stopping to assist local communities, encouraging wells, shared facilities or relief for those in need. One family of accounts remembers help in water-scarce settlements. These accounts express the Sikh ideal of seva and the expectation that religious leadership should improve everyday life. Their specific villages, conversations and miracles vary between later texts and local traditions. Rather than invent a single precisely dated incident, we should read them as attributed regional sakhis whose moral emphasis is clear but whose details are not independently verified.

This is consistent with earlier Gurus' work: the baoli at Goindwal, the pool at Amritsar and the development of community settlements. The continuity is historically meaningful even when an individual sakhi lacks contemporary corroboration.

8. GURBANI: COURAGE WITHOUT FEAR
Guru Tegh Bahadur's own compositions provide stronger direct evidence for his teaching than the wording of travel anecdotes. On Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji, Ang 1427, the Mahalla 9 salok begins:
ਜੋ ਨਰੁ ਦੁਖ ਮੈ ਦੁਖੁ ਨਹੀ ਮਾਨੈ ॥
A close rendering: 'The person who is not overcome by suffering amid suffering...' The full salok explores equanimity amid pleasure, pain, praise, blame and attachment. It should not be interpreted as indifference to injustice or as proof that the hymn was composed during any particular journey. The Ang identifies the text in the standard Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji, not a dated travel location. Read the surrounding text, not only its opening line.

The ninth Guru's bani also gives us a way to compare historical remembrance with scriptural evidence: the teaching is directly preserved, while an alleged conversation with a local ruler or villager may be attested only in much later writing.

9. THE MUGHAL SETTING
Aurangzeb ruled from 1658. The empire was large and administratively complex, with regional officials and competing political interests. It would be misleading to assume every interaction between a Sikh congregation and an imperial official was hostile. Nor should we deny that tensions developed during the period. The events of 1675 require close study of both Sikh and Mughal-source traditions; today's lesson is about the earlier years of travel and institution-building, not a premature retelling of the martyrdom.

10. KEY PEOPLE AND PLACES
Guru Tegh Bahadur Ji — ninth Sikh Guru, recognised in 1664.
Mata Nanaki Ji — the Guru's mother, commemorated in the name Chak Nanaki.
Mata Gujri Ji — the Guru's wife and mother of Gobind Rai.
Gobind Rai — born at Patna in 1666, later Guru Gobind Singh Ji.
Aurangzeb — Mughal emperor during the ninth Guruship.
Chak Nanaki / Anandpur Sahib — foothill settlement begun in 1665; later major Sikh centre.
Bakala — associated with the Guru's recognition.
Patna — city associated with the birth of Gobind Rai.
Assam and Bengal — eastern regions linked to the Guru's travels in historical tradition.

11. THREE RECALL QUESTIONS
1. What was Chak Nanaki named for, when was it founded, and why must we distinguish it from the later fortified Anandpur?
2. Where and when was Gobind Rai born, and why does this event help show the Sikh Panth's geographic reach?
3. What is the difference between the original Mahalla 9 salok on Ang 1427 and a later local sakhi about a stop on the Guru's journey?

12. RECAP
After his recognition in 1664, Guru Tegh Bahadur strengthened the Sikh Panth through settlement-building and extensive travel. Chak Nanaki was established in 1665 and later developed into Anandpur Sahib. The Guru's family was associated with Patna, where Gobind Rai was born in 1666. Eastern travel traditions connect the Guru with Bengal and Assam, but precise itineraries and particular political encounters remain debated. His bani on Ang 1427 provides direct scriptural testimony to spiritual steadiness, whereas many journey stories survive as later traditions. NEXT: the ninth Guru's later years, the circumstances leading to his execution in Delhi in 1675, and the differences between Sikh traditions and independently corroborated historical records.

SOURCES AND READING

J. S. Grewal, The Sikhs of the Punjab (Cambridge University Press), discussion of the later Gurus and seventeenth-century Sikh community.
Khushwant Singh, A History of the Sikhs, Volume I, sections on Guru Tegh Bahadur.
Encyclopaedia of Sikhism, Punjabi University, entries on Guru Tegh Bahadur, Anandpur Sahib and Patna Sahib: https://eos.learnpunjabi.org/

These are source recommendations and primary-text pointers, not fabricated page-specific citations or claims that every itinerary detail is verified.

title: Guru Tegh Bahadur Ji: Religious Freedom, Kashmiri Pandits and the Road to 1675
intro: The political and religious circumstances preceding Guru Tegh Bahadur Ji's execution in Delhi: Aurangzeb's policies, the Kashmiri Pandits' appeal tradition, early Sikh literary evidence and freedom of conscience.
record:
LESSON 27 — SATURDAY EVENING, 7 NOVEMBER 2026
GURU TEGH BAHADUR JI: RELIGIOUS FREEDOM, KASHMIRI PANDITS AND THE ROAD TO 1675
Period: 1669–1675 CE | Reading time: 9–10 minutes

CENTRAL QUESTION
How should we understand the circumstances preceding Guru Tegh Bahadur Ji's execution in 1675? What is supported by early historical evidence, and what belongs to later Sikh narratives?

1. CONTEXT
Guru Tegh Bahadur Ji became the ninth Guru in 1664. Previous lessons followed the establishment of Chak Nanaki in 1665 and journeys across northern and eastern India. The Sikh Panth had congregations far beyond Punjab, a developing network of religious centres, and a history of sometimes tense relations with Mughal power. In 1675, the Guru was executed in Delhi during Aurangzeb's reign. The martyrdom is foundational to Sikh memory, but reconstructing its immediate causes requires distinguishing imperial policy, regional politics, Sikh testimony, and later narrative traditions.

2. DATED TIMELINE
1658 — Aurangzeb consolidates power following the Mughal succession struggle.
1664 — Guru Tegh Bahadur recognised as ninth Guru after Guru Har Krishan's death.
1665 — Chak Nanaki established in the foothills, later connected with Anandpur Sahib.
1666 — Gobind Rai born at Patna.
1669 — Aurangzeb issues orders against certain temples and schools, recorded in the Persian chronicle Ma'asir-i-Alamgiri; implementation varied across places and times.
1670s — Guru Tegh Bahadur continues his leadership amid shifting Mughal and regional politics.
1675 — Sikh tradition locates the appeal of Kashmiri Brahmins and the Guru's decision to stand for freedom of conscience in this period.
November 1675 — Guru Tegh Bahadur executed in Delhi; 11 November is a commonly cited traditional date, but calendars and reconstructions differ.
1675 — Gobind Rai succeeds as tenth Guru.

3. THE EMPIRE WAS NOT ONE UNIFORM POLICY
Aurangzeb's reign saw both patronage and restrictions, negotiation and coercion. The emperor's policies toward temples, religious elites and local communities varied by region and political context. The 1669 order reported in Saqi Musta'id Khan's Ma'asir-i-Alamgiri is significant evidence of a restrictive measure, but it cannot by itself prove that every subject of the empire was under a single uninterrupted conversion campaign. Modern historical interpretation must account for local officials, fiscal conflicts, rebellion, and the language of imperial religious legitimacy. Avoid reducing all Hindus, Muslims or Sikhs to uniform political blocs.

4. KASHMIR AND THE APPEAL TRADITION
A central Sikh narrative says that Kashmiri Pandits, often led by Pandit Kirpa Ram (also rendered Kirpa Ram Datt), sought Guru Tegh Bahadur's help against coercive religious pressure. The tradition commonly names the Kashmir governor Iftikhar Khan. The delegation reportedly met the Guru at Chak Nanaki/Anandpur and asked him to defend their freedom of belief. Later accounts say that young Gobind Rai asked who could make the necessary sacrifice, and his father accepted that responsibility. This is an influential Sikh historical and devotional narrative; the detailed dialogue, membership of the delegation, and specific official orders are not independently established by a surviving contemporary meeting record. It would be equally mistaken to present the tradition as verbatim fact or to dismiss its importance in Sikh collective memory.

5. WHAT EARLY SIKH EVIDENCE SAYS
The near-contemporary Bachittar Natak, traditionally attributed to Guru Gobind Singh and included in the Dasam Granth corpus, praises Guru Tegh Bahadur for protecting tilak and janeu and giving his life for dharam. The frequently cited passage is 'ਤਿਲਕ ਜੰਞੂ ਰਾਖਾ ਪ੍ਰਭ ਤਾ ਕਾ' ('He protected the tilak and sacred thread'). This is NOT a verse of Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji and must not be assigned an Ang number there. The authorship, dating and textual history of Dasam Granth compositions are subjects of scholarship, so describe the attribution rather than pretending the manuscript questions are settled. The passage is strong evidence for how the sacrifice was framed in early Sikh literary memory, but it does not document every detail of the later Kashmiri delegation story.

6. THE ARREST: COMPETING RECONSTRUCTIONS
Accounts differ about the Guru's arrest location, route to Delhi, companions, detention and the precise charges. Sikh traditions often name Bhai Mati Das, Bhai Sati Das and Bhai Dayala among companions later martyred. Later narratives recount severe punishments inflicted on them. These figures are central to Sikh commemoration; individual speeches, torture sequences and dates vary across sources and should be labelled as traditional rather than treated as court transcripts. Some scholarly interpretations emphasise political fears about an influential regional religious leader; others foreground persecution and resistance to compelled conversion. The surviving evidence does not support a single simplified explanation that eliminates the other dimensions.

7. FREEDOM OF CONSCIENCE
In Sikh remembrance, Guru Tegh Bahadur defended the right of others to practise their faith, not merely his own community's privileges. The importance of the tilak and janeu imagery is precisely that these were markers of a tradition other than Sikh practice. The moral interpretation is that power should not compel belief. This interpretation is central to Sikh religious memory; a historian still distinguishes it from the separate question of what specific charges the Mughal administration recorded, and whether a surviving original execution order exists. We do not have a securely authenticated original imperial execution warrant spelling out all motives.

8. GURBANI: FEAR AND THE HUMAN CONDITION
Guru Tegh Bahadur's own bani in Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji is a primary source for his teachings, although it does not supply a dated account of the 1675 arrest. A Mahalla 9 salok on Ang 1427 begins 'ਜੋ ਨਰੁ ਦੁਖ ਮੈ ਦੁਖੁ ਨਹੀ ਮਾਨੈ ॥' — a person who is not overcome by suffering. Read the full salok in context: it speaks of spiritual steadiness amid pleasure, pain, praise, blame and attachment. Do not attribute its composition to a prison cell or to a final speech without evidence. The original text can be checked at https://www.gurugranthdarpan.net/1427.html. Guru Tegh Bahadur's teachings about fearlessness help readers interpret the later martyrdom, but scriptural meaning and event chronology are distinct kinds of evidence.

9. A SAKHI: THE YOUNG GOBIND RAI
In the traditional story of the Kashmiri petition, the Guru reflects that a great person's sacrifice is required. His son Gobind Rai asks who could be greater than his father, and the Guru accepts the path ahead. The narrative is preserved in later Sikh retellings and expresses the continuity between the ninth and tenth Gurus. Its exact dialogue cannot be verified independently. Treat it as a properly attributed sakhi, not a literal recorded conversation. It also prepares us to understand why Gobind Rai's succession in 1675 became inseparable from the memory of his father's death.

10. WHY 1675 IS A TURNING POINT
The execution occurred in the imperial capital, Delhi, and became a defining episode in Sikh accounts of conscience, courage and resistance to coercion. It shaped the tenth Guru's inherited responsibilities. Yet the later formation of the Khalsa in 1699 should not be described as an instantaneous or inevitable consequence of a single event; twenty-four years and many political and institutional developments intervened. In our next lesson we will examine the Delhi martyrdom itself, the associated sites, the traditions about the Guru's companions, and what the surviving evidence can and cannot establish.

KEY PEOPLE AND PLACES
Guru Tegh Bahadur Ji — ninth Sikh Guru; executed in Delhi in 1675.
Gobind Rai — son of the ninth Guru, later Guru Gobind Singh.
Aurangzeb — Mughal emperor (1658–1707).
Pandit Kirpa Ram — leader named in the Kashmiri delegation tradition.
Iftikhar Khan — Kashmir official named in some accounts; specifics require source caution.
Bhai Mati Das, Bhai Sati Das, Bhai Dayala — companions remembered as martyrs in Sikh tradition.
Chak Nanaki/Anandpur — associated with the traditional appeal.
Kashmir — region central to the delegation narrative.
Delhi — site of the Guru's execution.

THREE RECALL QUESTIONS
1. What does the Kashmiri Pandits' appeal tradition say, and which details cannot be independently verified as a contemporary transcript?
2. Why is the 'tilak and janeu' passage relevant, and why must it not be cited as an Ang of Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji?
3. What can Guru Tegh Bahadur's salok on Ang 1427 establish directly, and what can it not establish about the events of 1675?

RECAP
After founding Chak Nanaki and travelling widely, Guru Tegh Bahadur faced a tense imperial environment. Sikh tradition remembers Kashmiri Pandits appealing to him against coercion and his decision to defend freedom of conscience. Early Sikh literary remembrance celebrates his sacrifice; detailed delegation and prison narratives come largely through later accounts. Aurangzeb's policies must be studied in their uneven regional context. The Guru's own Gurbani on Ang 1427 speaks to spiritual steadiness but is not a dated account of his execution.
